options: Decide when to stop by checking stop_reason, not by parsing the reply text.
Return a tool failure to Claude as a tool_result with is_error set, and keep looping.
Cap the loop at a set number of iterations and hand off to a human when it's reached.
Raise max_tokens and continue the turn when stop_reason is max_tokens.

h.stem: Some support replies stop mid-sentence. Logs show those responses ended with stop_reason: "max_tokens", and the loop returns whatever text it has whenever the stop reason isn't tool_use. What should change?
why: Right when the loop guesses completion from phrases in the text. This loop already reads stop_reason; it just treats truncation as done.
Right when a tool error ends the loop. No tool failed here; the reply was cut off.
Right when the agent can loop forever. This agent stops too early, not too late.
max_tokens means the reply was truncated, not finished. Give it room and continue instead of returning a partial answer.

p.stem: When the order-lookup tool times out, the loop exits and the agent replies “I couldn't complete that,” even though a cached-orders tool could have answered. What should change?
why: Right when the loop guesses completion from the text. Here the exit is caused by the tool failure.
Errors are information: send the failure back so Claude can try the cached-orders tool.
Right when the agent loops without progress. Here it gives up after one failure.
Right when replies are truncated. Nothing was cut off here; a tool failed.

options: Block the refund tool in code until verify_identity has succeeded this session.
Add few-shot examples showing how the agent should word its identity-check request.
Escalate with a structured summary: customer ID, issue, steps taken, what's needed.
Record completed steps in session state so later checks don't ask for them again.

h.stem: Escalations reach human agents as “customer needs help with a refund.” The humans re-ask for the order number, the verification result and what the agent already tried, so customers repeat themselves. What fixes this?
why: Right when refunds can happen before verification. The workflow order is fine here; the handoff is thin.
Right when the agent asks for verification in confusing ways. The problem here is what the human receives.
The human starts without the conversation, so the handoff must carry the facts and progress explicitly.
Right when the agent itself re-asks for completed steps. Here the humans lack the information.

p.stem: An audit finds 3% of refunds were issued before identity verification, despite a bold system-prompt rule. Verification is a compliance requirement. What fixes this?
why: A requirement with compliance stakes needs a guarantee in code, not a more emphatic instruction.
Right when the wording of the check confuses customers. Examples still leave the order probabilistic.
Right when humans receive thin handoffs. This is about the order of the agent's own steps.
Right when completed checks get repeated. Here a required check is sometimes skipped.

options: A PreToolUse hook that blocks refund calls above the approval limit.
A PostToolUse hook that masks card numbers to the last four digits.
A PostToolUse hook that converts each backend's dates to ISO 8601.
A system-prompt line asking the agent to suggest the cheaper shipping option first.

h.stem: Order data comes from three backends: one returns Unix timestamps, one “MM/DD/YY”, one ISO 8601. The agent sometimes gets return-window eligibility wrong when comparing dates across them. Which addition fits best?
why: Right when an action must be stopped before it runs. The problem here is inconsistent data coming back.
Right when sensitive values appear in results. The dates here are safe; they're just inconsistent.
Normalize tool results to one format before the model reasons over them.
Right for a soft preference where an occasional miss is fine. Date comparison needs consistent data.

p.stem: Policy now requires manager approval for refunds over $500. When customers push hard, the agent sometimes issues larger refunds anyway. Which addition fits best?
why: A financial limit needs to be enforced before the call runs, every time.
Right when sensitive data appears in tool results. Here the issue is an action that shouldn't run.
Right when results arrive in mixed formats. Here the issue is an action that shouldn't run.
Right for soft preferences. A refund limit with financial stakes needs a guarantee.

options: Extract every request into a checklist first, then resolve each one in turn.
Run a fixed sequence: classify, look up the order, then draft the reply.
Let the agent pick each next step from what the previous tool returned.
Give each request to its own subagent and run them in parallel.

h.stem: Customers often send one message with three or four requests, each needing a quick lookup on the same account. The agent resolves the first and forgets the rest. What design fits best?
why: Make every request explicit up front so none is dropped, then work through them with the shared account context.
Right when every ticket follows the same stages. These messages vary in how many requests they hold.
Right when the path depends on findings. Here the problem is dropping known requests.
Right for heavy, independent work. These are quick lookups on one account, so subagents add overhead and split shared context.

p.stem: Warranty claims follow the same three steps in the same order every time, and auditors want each claim handled identically. What design fits best?
why: Right when one message holds several requests. A warranty claim is a single, predictable task.
A predictable, identical sequence is what a fixed pipeline is for, and it's easy to audit.
Right when the path depends on what turns up. Here the path never changes, and auditors want it fixed.
Right for heavy, independent sub-tasks. These steps depend on each other in order.

options: Escalate with a structured summary: customer ID, issue, steps taken, what's needed.
Require a code-checked supervisor approval before any account closure runs.
Keep verified facts in a case-facts block that is re-sent every turn.
Hand the conversation to a human when the customer explicitly asks for one.

h.stem: Customers who type “let me talk to a person” are told “I can help with that myself” and kept with the agent. Complaints are rising, although the agent often could have solved the issue. What should change?
why: Right when the human lacks context after a handoff. Here the handoff never happens.
Right for an irreversible action needing sign-off. Nothing irreversible is involved here.
Right when facts get lost over a long chat. Here the customer's request is being overridden.
An explicit request for a human is a reason to hand off, even when the agent could solve it.

p.stem: Account closures can't be undone, and legal requires a supervisor's sign-off before one runs. The agent occasionally closes accounts directly. What should change?
why: Right when handoffs lack context. Here the agent skips a required step.
An irreversible action with legal stakes needs its prerequisite enforced in code.
Right when the agent forgets facts. Here it skips a required approval.
Right when a customer asks for a person. Here the problem is an unapproved action.

options: A PreToolUse hook that blocks Bash commands touching the production config.
A PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter on every file Claude edits.
A CLAUDE.md note describing the team's preferred commit-message style.
A PostToolUse hook that trims test output to the failures before Claude sees it.

h.stem: The test suite prints thousands of lines per run. After a few runs Claude's context is full of passing-test output and it loses track of the task. Which addition fits best?
why: Right when an action must never run. Nothing dangerous is happening here.
Right when edits drift from the formatter. The problem here is bloated tool output.
Right for a convention where occasional drift is cheap. It doesn't change what tools return.
Trim tool results to what matters before they reach the model, so they stop crowding the context.

p.stem: PRs keep failing review because about one in ten of Claude's edits ignores the project's formatter settings. Formatting must match exactly. Which addition fits best?
why: Right when an action must be blocked. Formatting needs to be applied, not blocked.
Run the formatter after every edit so the result is correct every time.
Right for a convention where an occasional miss is fine. Exact formatting needs a guarantee.
Right when tool output floods the context. This is about the files Claude writes.

options: Have Claude write a plan, then implement it step by step against that plan.
Review one file per pass, then run a final pass over cross-file consistency.
Make the change directly in one pass, because it's small and well understood.
Explore the codebase first, then decide the next steps from what turns up.

h.stem: Claude reviews a 40-file pull request in one pass. It misses problems in the later files and contradicts itself about the same pattern in different files. What approach fits best?
why: Right for building a known multi-step change. This is a review whose attention is spread too thin.
Per-file passes keep attention focused, and a separate pass catches what crosses files.
Right for a small, clear change. A 40-file review is neither.
Right when you don't yet know where to look. Here the files to review are known.

p.stem: The build fails intermittently and nobody knows which part of the codebase causes it. What approach fits best?
why: Right when the steps are known up front. Here you don't yet know what to change.
Right for reviewing a large, known set of files. Here the cause isn't located yet.
Right for a small, well-understood change. The cause here is unknown.
When the cause is unknown, investigate first and let the findings decide the next step.

options: Have the coordinator split the topic into distinct subtopics before delegating.
Have the coordinator check results against the question and re-delegate the gaps.
Route all subagent output through the coordinator, not directly between subagents.
Give each subagent only the tools that its role needs.

h.stem: The coordinator's initial split looks sound, but reports still miss things that only become visible once results arrive, such as a major study that several sources cite but nobody searched for. What change fits best?
why: Right when the first split leaves parts of the question out. The split here is fine; the gaps appear later.
Evaluate what came back and send follow-up work for the gaps, so coverage improves as findings arrive.
Right when subagents talk to each other and coordination breaks. Here the issue is coverage.
Right when subagents misuse each other's tools. Here the issue is coverage.

p.stem: The web-search subagent keeps calling the document-analysis tools, and the analysis subagent keeps searching the web. Work is duplicated and the budget runs out. What change fits best?
why: Right when the split misses parts of the question. Here the roles are blurred by their tools.
Right when coverage gaps appear after results arrive. Here the issue is role overlap.
Right when subagents bypass the coordinator. Here each one simply has tools outside its role.
Scoping tools to each role keeps subagents on their job and makes selection reliable.

options: Put the earlier findings and their sources directly in the subagent's prompt.
Have subagents return structured results: claim, source URL and date for each.
Spawn the independent searches in the same turn so they run in parallel.
Write the subagent's prompt as goals and quality criteria, not fixed steps.

h.stem: The coordinator merges subagent reports, but each report is free prose. The final report can't say which source supports which claim, or how recent it is. What change fits best?
why: Right when a subagent never received the earlier results. Here the results arrive; their sources get lost.
Separating each claim from its source metadata lets the coordinator keep attribution through synthesis.
Right when independent work runs one after another. Here the issue is attribution.
Right when rigid steps stop subagents adapting. Here the issue is the shape of what comes back.

p.stem: The synthesis subagent is asked to “write up the findings so far” and produces a confident report with invented details. It never received the search results. What change fits best?
why: Subagents don't share the coordinator's context; the findings must be passed in the prompt.
Right when results lose their sources. Here the subagent got no results at all.
Right when independent subagents run one after another. This one lacks its input.
Right when step-by-step prompts make subagents rigid. Without the findings, no prompt style helps.

options: Use a fixed pipeline: search, then analyze, then synthesize, in that order.
Let the coordinator choose the next subagent based on what the last one found.
Run the searches for independent subtopics in parallel subagents.
Handle the whole request in a single agent with one context.

h.stem: Most requests turn out to be quick factual questions that two or three searches answer. The multi-agent setup adds minutes of overhead and most of the cost. What design fits these requests best?
why: Right when every request runs through the same stages. Three stages are still overhead for a two-search answer.
Right when findings change what to do next. These answers don't need that.
Right when there are several independent subtopics. A quick factual question has one.
A small task doesn't need delegation; one agent is faster and cheaper here.

p.stem: Investigations often turn up a lead, such as a name or a dataset, that changes what should be searched next. The current fixed pipeline can't follow it. What design fits best?
why: That's the current design, and it can't follow new leads.
When findings change the path, decide each next step from what came back.
Right when subtopics are known and independent. Here the next search depends on the last result.
Right for small tasks. These investigations are open-ended.

options: Have subagents report to the coordinator, which decides what to pass on.
Have the coordinator check each claim's source before including it.
Send a failed subtopic back to a subagent with a narrower query.
Give the coordinator a limit on research rounds before it must synthesize.

h.stem: Some reports take hours. The coordinator keeps finding “one more angle” and re-delegating long after the question has been answered well. What change fits best?
why: Right when subagents talk directly and the coordinator loses track. Here the coordinator is the one that won't stop.
Right when unsupported claims reach the report. Here the problem is open-ended looping.
Right when a subtopic came back empty. Here everything is answered; the coordinator just keeps going.
A bound on rounds forces synthesis once coverage is good enough.

p.stem: When a search subagent finds nothing for one subtopic, the coordinator quietly drops it, and the report has a hole nobody notices. What change fits best?
why: Right when subagents bypass the coordinator. Here the coordinator receives the result and drops it.
Right when claims lack support. Here a subtopic has no claims at all.
An empty result calls for a retry with a better query, not silent omission.
Right when the coordinator won't stop. Here it stops too soon on one subtopic.

options: Add the Task (Agent) tool to the coordinator's allowedTools.
Include the earlier agent's complete findings in the subagent's prompt.
Define each subagent with its own description, prompt and tool list.
Spawn the subagents in the same response so they run in parallel.

h.stem: The coordinator's prompt tells it to delegate, but it does all the searching itself. Logs show the subagent-spawning tool never appears among its available tools. What change fits best?
why: The coordinator can only spawn subagents if the Task tool (now called Agent) is available to it.
Right when a subagent lacks earlier results. Here no subagent is ever spawned.
Right when subagents are generic or overlap. Here none can be spawned at all.
Right when subagents run one after another. Here none run.

p.stem: The coordinator spawns subagents for four independent subtopics, one after another across four turns. Each request takes about four times longer than it should. What change fits best?
why: Right when the coordinator can't spawn subagents. It can; it just does so one at a time.
Right when a subagent lacks context. Here the subtopics are independent.
Right when subagent roles are unclear. Here the roles work; the timing doesn't.
Several subagent calls in one response run in parallel.

options: A PreToolUse hook that denies file writes outside the project directory.
A PostToolUse hook that maps the internal API's responses onto one schema.
A PreToolUse hook that adds the required team label to the tool's input.
A skill containing the team's release steps, which developers run on demand.

h.stem: Every ticket Claude files through the tracker tool must carry the “eng-tools” label. Claude leaves it off about one time in eight, even with an instruction in CLAUDE.md. What fits best?
why: Right when an action must be blocked. Here the action is fine; its input needs a fix.
Right when responses vary in shape. Here the problem is what goes in, not what comes back.
A pre-call hook can modify the input, so the label is there on every call.
Right for an on-demand workflow. A required field needs to be enforced on every call.

p.stem: Developers want a repeatable way to cut a release that any teammate can invoke when needed, with the team's steps written down once. What fits best?
why: Right when an action must be prevented. Nothing needs blocking here.
Right when responses vary in shape. This is about a procedure.
Right when every call needs a fixed input. Here developers want a procedure they run on request.
A skill packages a repeatable procedure that people invoke on demand.

options: Use the Explore subagent to search the codebase and return a summary.
Pass the relevant file paths and the decisions so far in the subagent's prompt.
Give the subagent read-only tools so it can't modify anything.
Ask the subagent to return its findings in a fixed structured format.

h.stem: After a long discussion about the CSV parser, a developer has Claude hand “write tests for the parser we discussed” to a subagent. The subagent writes tests for a different parser. What fixes this?
why: Right when exploration floods the main context. Here the subagent lacks the discussion.
A subagent starts without the conversation, so the specifics must be in its prompt.
Right when the subagent shouldn't change files. Here it needs to write tests.
Right when the caller must parse results reliably. Here the subagent worked on the wrong target.

p.stem: In a large, unfamiliar repository, the main session fills with file listings and search output before any real work starts. What fixes this?
why: Exploration in a separate context returns only a summary, keeping the main session clean.
Right when a subagent lacks specifics. Here the main session is overloaded.
Right for review work that shouldn't modify files. Here the problem is context bloat.
Right when the output format is unreliable. Here the problem is volume in the main session.

options: Return a tool's error to Claude with is_error set so it can try another approach.
Check stop_reason to decide whether to run tools or return the answer.
Run every tool_use block in a response and return all the results together.
Send the full message history, including tool results, with each request.

h.stem: Claude asks to read two files in one response. The internal tool's loop runs only the first request, and the next API call is rejected. What should change?
why: Right when a tool failure ends the loop. Here a requested call never ran.
Right when the loop guesses completion from text. Here it mishandles a turn with two calls.
Each tool_use needs a matching tool_result; return them all in the next user message.
Right when earlier turns go missing. Here the current turn's second call is the problem.

p.stem: In the internal assistant, follow-up questions are answered as if earlier tool results never happened. The loop sends only the newest user message with each request. What should change?
why: Right when errors end the loop. Here context is missing.
Right when the loop guesses completion. Here context is missing.
Right when some tool calls go unanswered. Here past results are dropped.
The API is stateless; each request must carry the whole conversation.

options: Have the pipeline block the merge in code when the review reports a blocking issue.
Add explicit criteria to the review prompt for what counts as blocking.
Make the secret scan a required step that must pass before the review job starts.
Post findings as inline comments that cite the file and line.

h.stem: Policy says no AI review may run on code that hasn't passed the secret scanner. The workflow sometimes starts both jobs at once, and the review occasionally reads a leaked key. What fixes this?
why: Right when findings are ignored at merge time. The problem here is what runs first.
Right when the review misjudges severity. Here the order of steps is wrong.
A required prerequisite must be enforced in the pipeline, not left to timing.
Right when findings are hard to act on. Here the review shouldn't run yet.

p.stem: The review flags blocking issues correctly, but teams merge anyway because the job only posts a comment. Blocking issues must stop the merge. What fixes this?
why: A rule that must hold needs enforcement in code; a comment can be ignored.
Right when the review over-flags. Here its verdicts are right; they're ignored.
Right when the review runs on unscanned code. Here the issue is what happens after.
Right when findings are hard to locate. Here they're found and ignored.

options: Review each changed file in its own pass, then one pass on cross-file interactions.
Review the whole diff in a single pass, with the PR description as context.
Run separate passes for security, performance and style.
Review only the files that changed since the last reviewed commit.

h.stem: Most pull requests touch two or three files. The multi-pass review takes six minutes each, single-pass reviews of diffs this size have been accurate, and the team wants fast feedback. What fits best?
why: Right for large diffs where attention spreads thin. Small diffs don't need it.
A small diff fits comfortably in one pass, which gives fast feedback without losing accuracy.
Right when one concern crowds out the others. That hasn't happened at this size.
Right when re-reviews repeat old findings. Here the problem is speed.

p.stem: After each push, the review re-reports issues on files that didn't change, burying the new findings. What fits best?
why: Right for large diffs. Here the problem is re-reviewing unchanged files.
Right for small diffs. It still re-reviews everything.
Right when one concern crowds out the others. Here the problem is repetition.
Limit each re-review to what changed so old findings don't repeat.
